children: By Andrew Tangel and Drew FitzGerald
The Federal Aviation Administration has halted installations of routers at the center of communications disruptions that prompted a rare, nationwide ground stop.

FAA officials said the pause will be in place while the agency assesses what went wrong Friday — an ordeal that resulted in nearly 20,000 flights being canceled and thousands more delayed — with equipment at its facilities.
"I feel highly confident that we won't repeat this level of disruption," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Tuesday at a press conference in Washington, D.C.

On Friday, L3Harris Technologies, the government contractor in charge of running the FAA's antiquated air-traffic communications network, installed a new router at a radio transmitter site in southern Arkansas. That router appears to have begun spewing out data that swamped the network, leading to interference with communications between pilots and air-traffic controllers around the country, federal officials have said.
Bedford said the agency was still investigating what prompted the router issues.

"Based on what we know and have been told by others, our equipment was working as configured," said a spokesman from HPE, corporate parent of the router's manufacturer. "The FAA is assessing the configuration and performance of all infrastructure involved to determine the cause."

The installation of the router was part of work the FAA has been doing with L3Harris to upgrade its communications network, a multiyear, multibillion process to stop using obsolete copper wires and move into the fiber-optic age.

A group of Democratic senators, including Senate Commerce Committee ranking member Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, called on the FAA to halt installation of the new routers and demanded a clear accounting of what went wrong.

The FAA wants to get older equipment out of the system and has a brisk schedule to do so, according to people familiar with the matter. Not only is the FAA's copper-wire-laden network increasingly prone to failure, but local phone companies are cutting off service, the FAA official said.

One element of the upgrade: Installing new routers from HPE's Juniper Networks as a stopgap while the FAA completes its full transition to a modern network and systems, industry and government officials said.

Bedford said each router installation undergoes a comprehensive risk assessment. But he said the agency would examine its processes, including how the devices were tested before being deployed into the nation's air-traffic system.

Installation of the new Juniper routers began in July, people familiar with the matter said. Bedford said 69 of them had been deployed so far. Those installations had occurred without a major hiccup, until Friday.
Start and stop

L3Harris had sought to install a new router in El Dorado, Ark. The FAA was the only remaining customer on the copper lines there, and service was slated to be discontinued as soon as next year, the FAA official said.
L3Harris proposed to do the installation during the day — a busy time for flying. The FAA approved the move, the people said.

The communications network overseen by L3Harris is part of the operational backbone of the nation's air-traffic system. It carries radar, voice, navigation and weather data that the controllers and pilots rely on. It is a live nationwide system, so there is no off switch.

The FAA has often scheduled maintenance work overnight to minimize disruptions on air travel, as was the case in June when work by L3Harris led to brief radio and radar interruptions at a facility that oversees airspace around Newark, N.J.

For the Arkansas work, L3Harris asked that the equipment installation work happen between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. ET, the agency official said. L3Harris outlined its plan and procedures for the installation to the FAA, according to people familiar with the matter.

An FAA representative helped an L3Harris employee — an Air Force veteran — gain access to the Arkansas site. The agency official said the FAA didn't supervise the work on the L3Harris equipment. Bedford described him as a "highly trained, certified engineer" who was monitored by an FAA technician.
"I'm told [he's] generally a confident guy doing the work that he's done dozens and dozens of times before," Bedford said.
After the new router was installed, the agency official said, the FAA brought the radio site back online and monitored it against the preapproved risk-assessment.
Shortly after 3 p.m. ET, the problems started. Pilots began to report static and cracking in their communications. The nationwide ground stop was ordered at 3:47 p.m.
The FAA identified the router in Arkansas and another one in Amarillo, Texas, as overloading the broader communication system with data, spurring disruptions to radios and radar.
Older routers manufactured by Cisco Systems elsewhere in the air-traffic control system started getting overloaded with data, the official said.

The FAA later stabilized the air-traffic system by isolating the Arkansas and Texas sites. The specific broadcasting feature on the Juniper routers has been disabled to prevent future disruptions, the people said.
